title: Controlling Intertwined Electronic Orders in FeSe with Exfoliation
authors: Wenyao Liu, Gabriel Natale, Kyung-Mo Kim, Birender Singh, Piyush Sakrikar, Stephen D. Funni, Leo Kondo, Augustin Davignon, Antoine de Lagrave, Kota Ishihara, Michael Geiwitz, Maia G. Vergniory, Takasada Shibauchi, Jun Sung Kim, Michał Papaj, Judy J. Cha, Kenneth S. Burch†
abstract: Controlling intertwined electronic orders in two-dimensional superconductors offers an effective route to answering fundamental questions and engineering new quantum devices. However, tuning the balance between competing orders typically requires complex chemistry, strain, or interface engineering. Here, we show that a pristine alternative is the dimensional reduction of the unconventional superconductor FeSe. Exfoliation suppresses the bulk electronic nematic response and switches the superconducting symmetry from bulk s-wave to d-wave-dominant. Transport, electron microscopy, and Raman spectroscopy establish the substantial weakening of nematic order in thin flakes. To probe superconductivity, we perform angle-dependent Andreev reflection spectroscopy on pristine crystal edges. As the junction's orientation is rotated, the spectra evolve from zero-energy bound states to coherence peaks. The injection angle, field, and temperature dependence, along with theoretical modeling, confirm that exfoliation switches the superconducting symmetry. Our results suggest a versatile superconducting platform for engineering quantum orders and provide fresh insights into the underlying pairing mechanisms.
summary: This work demonstrates that physically thinning the superconductor FeSe via exfoliation acts as a powerful tool to manipulate its electronic state. Experimentally, this process suppresses the bulk nematic order and spectroscopically confirms a symmetry switch in the superconducting pairing from s-wave to d-wave-dominant. This establishes FeSe thin flakes as a versatile platform for engineering quantum superconducting orders.
main_problem: The study investigates how controlling the electronic structure via exfoliation can tune the competing electronic orders (nematic and superconducting) in the unconventional superconductor FeSe.
main_result: Exfoliation suppresses the bulk electronic nematic response and fundamentally switches the superconducting symmetry from bulk s-wave to a d-wave-dominant pairing state.
method: The research employs a combination of experimental techniques, including angle-dependent Andreev reflection spectroscopy, Raman scattering, and transport measurements, complemented by theoretical modeling using the 2D-BTK model.
model_or_system: The physical system is Iron Selenide (FeSe), an unconventional superconductor. The theoretical framework involves modeling the superconducting order parameter (sOP) symmetry, often using extensions of the 2D-BTK model to account for $s+d$-wave pairing.
key_observables: Superconducting symmetry (s-wave vs. d-wave), nematic order strength (probed by Raman response), superconducting gap size ($\Delta$), and critical temperature ($T_c$).
important_parameters: Flake thickness (dimensional reduction), magnetic field ($B$), temperature ($T$), and the nematic interaction strength ($g_{nem}$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that exfoliation provides a clean tuning knob for electronic orders, and that Andreev reflection measurements can be accurately modeled using the 2D-BTK formalism.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the suppression of nematic signatures in thin flakes via Raman maps, the transition from coherence peaks to Zero-Bias Conductance Peaks (ZBCP) in ARS spectra, and the thickness dependence of superconducting gap components.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the problem of controlling intertwined orders, then presenting evidence from transport and Raman spectroscopy showing nematic suppression upon exfoliation, followed by definitive proof of symmetry switching using angle-dependent Andreev reflection spectroscopy, and concluding with theoretical modeling of the resulting pairing symmetry.
why_interesting: The ability to tune superconducting pairing symmetry using purely structural/dimensional control (exfoliation) is highly relevant to understanding emergent quantum states in strongly correlated materials, providing a clean platform for studying pairing mechanisms.
